description:
Odysseia (Οδύσσεια) is Greek for a long journey of discovery, and Space Apps is exactly that: 48 hours from raw NASA data to a working idea. We’re a collaborative team that shares ideas openly and learns from each other.

Looking for: science/data people, UI/UX designers, storytellers for the pitch, and anyone curious and willing to contribute, at any level. Join us and let’s make the journey together!
summary:
Odysseia is a browser-based mission-control tool for choosing Artemis landing sites and launch dates at the Moon’s south pole.

Near the pole, the Moon’s 1.54° axial tilt keeps the Sun grazing the horizon, so crater rims cast long shadows, and libration can suddenly cut the line of sight to Earth. A ten-meter shift in position or a launch slip can decide whether a site is lit. Odysseia brings this together in one place instead of scattered data tables.

Built on NASA LOLA 20 m/pixel elevation data and ephemeris calculations, it works out sunlight and Earth visibility for each site. You can view a site on a 3D Moon globe, as local 3D terrain, as a 360° skyline, and on a sky dial. A 29.5-day timeline shows when a site is lit, a compare view puts up to four sites side by side, and scorecards summarize the trade-offs.

Everything runs in the browser at 60 FPS, and solar elevation is validated against NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.0018°. It is made for engineers, scientists and educators who need to choose landing zones with confidence.
details:
What it does
Odysseia is a browser-based mission-control tool for comparing candidate landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. For any date between 2024 and 2030, it shows how much sunlight a site gets and when it has a line of sight to Earth, so planners can see the trade-off between solar power and communication blackouts.

How it works
Three parts run entirely in the browser. First, an ephemeris engine computes where the Sun and Earth are, using the IAU 2009 / Mean Earth lunar reference frame. Second, a custom raycaster scans NASA LOLA 20 m/pixel elevation data (LDEM_80S_20M), including the Moon’s curvature, to build a 360° horizon from a 2 m lander mast. Third, results are shown in four synchronized views: a 3D Moon globe with a live day/night line, 3D local terrain with solar shadows, a 360° skyline panorama, and a sky dial that plots the Sun and Earth against the local horizon.

Benefits
A single screen replaces scattered spreadsheets. A 29.53-day timeline shows lit and dark periods, a compare view puts up to four sites side by side with differences in illumination, blackout hours, slope and temperature extremes, and a date-sweep heatmap checks 48 landing dates across a year to find workable launch windows. Calculations run in Web Workers at 60 FPS, with no server.

Intended impact
We wanted to close the gap between raw scientific data and the decisions mission planners actually make. Odysseia is meant for engineers, researchers, educators and students who need to evaluate landing zones and anticipate loss-of-signal periods for Artemis-era missions and commercial landers.

Tools
TypeScript, GLSL and Python (data pipeline); React 18, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Vite and Tailwind CSS; Comlink and Zustand; Astronomy Engine for ephemerides; data from NASA LRO LOLA, the JPL Horizons API, the LROC WAC global mosaic and the USGS Planetary Gazetteer. 175 automated tests with Vitest, plus Playwright.

What’s creative about it
It connects the global view, a local 20 m terrain mesh and a first-person skyline in one workspace. The interface is a charcoal and amber telemetry-style display with two modes: a plain-language Overview for stakeholders and a technical view for engineers. A short guided tour explains the polar constraints in under a minute.

What we considered
Accuracy: the LOLA grid was aligned to Lunar Laser Ranging retroreflector positions to within 14.1 m (under one pixel), and the ephemeris was checked against NASA JPL Horizons at 100 benchmark points, with an RMSE of 0.0018° for Sun elevation and 0.0219° for Earth elevation. Honesty: the app labels which sites use real LOLA polar data and which use synthetic baseline profiles. Reliability: it detects WebGL support, explains how to enable hardware acceleration, and supports full keyboard navigation.
